items.prompt: A white rook stood on a1 and has been taken off the board. Tap every square it attacked. A square holding an enemy piece counts, but the rook cannot see past it.

claims.statement: A rook on a1 attacks exactly a2, a3, a4, b1, c1 and d1.

hints: A rook slides along its file and its rank until something stops it.
Go up the a-file first, then along the first rank. Which pieces block the way?
The pawn on a4 and the knight on d1 are the first pieces in the way; the rook attacks them and goes no further.
items.explain: Along the a-file the rook sees a2, a3 and the pawn on a4, then stops. Along the first rank it sees b1, c1 and the knight on d1, then stops.

items.prompt: A white king stood on e4 and has been taken off the board. Tap every square it attacked.

claims.statement: A king on e4 attacks exactly d3, e3, f3, d4, f4, d5, e5 and f5.

hints: A king steps one square in any direction.
Count the squares in a ring around e4.
The ring has eight squares: three above, three below and one on each side.
items.explain: A king attacks every neighbouring square. In the middle of the board that is a ring of eight: d3, e3, f3, d4, f4, d5, e5 and f5.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white pawn on e4 attacks. (Remember: a pawn attacks diagonally, not straight ahead.)

claims.statement: A white pawn on e4 attacks exactly d5 and f5.

hints: A pawn moves straight but captures on the diagonals.
White pawns capture towards the black side of the board.
The two squares are diagonally forward, one file to each side of e4.
items.explain: A white pawn attacks the two squares diagonally in front of it. From e4 those are d5 and f5, which here hold a black knight and a black bishop. The square e5 in front of the pawn is not attacked.

items.prompt: Is the square e7 light or dark? Decide from the name before you look at the board.

claims.statement: A pawn on e7 stands on a dark square.

hints: The corner square a1 is dark and colours alternate.
Turn e into 5 (a=1 ... h=8) and add the rank number 7.
5+7=12. An even sum means a dark square.
items.explain: Add the file number (a=1 to h=8) and the rank number: an even sum is a dark square. For e7 that is 5+7=12, so it is dark.

items.prompt: A white pawn stands on b4 and a black pawn on e4. Are b4 and e4 squares of the same colour? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The white pawn on b4 stands on a dark square.
The black pawn on e4 stands on a light square.

hints: Both squares are on the fourth rank. Moving along a rank changes the colour with every step.
b to e is three steps along the rank. Is three even or odd?
An odd number of steps lands on the other colour.
items.explain: Squares alternate in colour along a rank, so two squares on the same rank are the same colour only when an even number of files lies between them. b to e is three files, so b4 and e4 differ: b4 is dark and e4 is light.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white bishop on c4 can legally move to. Captures count.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 can move to exactly a2, b3, d3, e2, f1, b5, a6 and d5.

hints: A bishop slides along diagonals and stops at the first piece in its way.
Follow all four diagonals from c4 one at a time.
Three diagonals run to the edge; the fourth stops on the black pawn at d5, which the bishop can capture.
items.explain: Down-left: b3, a2. Down-right: d3, e2, f1. Up-left: b5, a6. Up-right: d5, where the black pawn stands, and the bishop may capture it but not go beyond.

items.prompt: A white bishop stands on c1. Can it reach f8 in exactly two moves (Black does not move)? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The bishop can play Bh6.
After Bh6 the bishop attacks f8, so a second move reaches it.

hints: First check the colour of the two squares: can a bishop ever get from one to the other?
c1 and f8 are both dark squares, so the colour is no obstacle. Look for a square halfway.
From c1 a long diagonal runs to h6; from h6 look back along the other diagonal.
items.explain: Bc1-h6 uses the long diagonal, and from h6 the bishop attacks f8 along the diagonal through g7. Two moves, same colour, and a clear path both times.

items.prompt: A white queen stood on a1 and has been taken off the board. Tap every square it attacked. Enemy pieces count but block the line behind them.

claims.statement: A queen on a1 attacks exactly b1, c1, a2 to a8, b2, c3 and d4.

hints: The queen combines the rook and the bishop. From a1 she has three lines.
The file runs to the top edge. The rank and the long diagonal each meet an enemy piece.
Rank: stop at the bishop on c1. Diagonal: stop at the pawn on d4.
items.explain: The queen sees a2 to a8 up the file, b1 and the bishop on c1 along the rank, and b2, c3 and the pawn on d4 along the diagonal: twelve squares in all.

items.prompt: How many black pieces attack the square e5, where the white knight stands?

claims.statement: Three black pieces attack e5.

hints: Check each black piece in turn and ask whether it can reach e5 in one move.
The black bishop, knight and rook are all candidates. Are any of their paths blocked?
None of the three paths is blocked: bishop along the diagonal, knight by its jump, rook down the file.
items.explain: The bishop on b8 sees e5 along the diagonal through c7 and d6, the knight on c6 jumps to e5, and the rook on e8 sees it down the open e-file. The king on h8 is too far. That makes three.

items.prompt: Tap every square that is attacked both by the white knight on g5 and by the white bishop on c4.

claims.statement: The knight on g5 attacks exactly e4, e6, f3, f7, h3, h7.
The bishop on c4 attacks exactly a2, a6, b3, b5, d3, d5, e2, e6, f1, f7.

hints: Work out each piece's squares separately before comparing.
The knight on g5 has six squares and the bishop on c4 has nine. Which names appear in both lists?
Both shared squares are right next to the black king.
items.explain: The knight reaches e4, e6, f3, f7, h3, h7; the bishop reaches a2, a6, b3, b5, d3, d5, e2, e6, f1, f7. The shared squares are e6 and f7.

items.prompt: Which white piece has more legal moves: the knight on d5 or the bishop on b2?

claims.statement: The knight on d5 has 8 legal moves.
The bishop on b2 has 8 legal moves.

hints: Count each piece's moves one piece at a time, not by guessing which type is stronger.
The knight is in the centre with nothing in its way. The bishop has a long open diagonal and a short one too.
Both counts come out the same.
items.explain: The knight on d5 has all eight of its jumps free. The bishop on b2 has a1, c1 and a3 on the short diagonals and c3, d4, e5, f6 and the capture on g7 on the long one: also eight.

items.prompt: A white bishop stands on c1 and a white pawn on e3. Can the bishop reach h6 in one move? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The bishop on c1 can move to exactly a3, b2 and d2.
Bh6 is not legal.

hints: h6 is on the same diagonal as c1. Is anything in the way?
Trace the diagonal square by square: d2, e3, f4, g5, h6.
The pawn on e3 stands on that diagonal.
items.explain: c1 and h6 share a diagonal, but the white pawn on e3 sits between them and a bishop cannot jump over its own pawn. The bishop stops at d2.

items.prompt: A white rook stood on d1 and has been taken off the board. Tap every square it could legally move to.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 can move to exactly a1, b1, c1, e1, f1, d2 and d3.

hints: A rook cannot move onto a square holding its own piece or beyond it.
Look along the first rank in both directions, then up the d-file.
The king on g1 stops the rook on the right; the pawn on d4 stops it going up.
items.explain: To the left the rook can reach c1, b1 and a1; to the right e1 and f1, because the king stands on g1. Up the file it reaches d2 and d3, and the pawn on d4 blocks the rest.

items.prompt: How many legal moves does the white knight on e4 have?

claims.statement: The knight on e4 has no legal moves.
The knight attacks 8 squares even though it cannot move.

hints: A knight in the open usually has eight jumps. Is anything stopping this one?
Look at the line between the black rook and the white king.
The knight stands on that line; if it leaves, the king is in check.
items.explain: The black rook on e8 and the white king on e1 are on the same file with only the knight between them. Any knight move would expose the king to check, so none is legal, although it still attacks eight squares.
